q1.answer: The cleft is on the left side.

q2.answer: The gap is in the bone of the gum, next to the front teeth, in the upper jaw. It is called the alveolar cleft.

q3.answer: The small tooth next to the front tooth (lateral incisor) is missing. About half of children with a cleft do not have this tooth on the cleft side.

q4.answer: The eye tooth needs bone to grow into and come down. The graft gives it bone to come down into.
q4.where: Sheet 1, The eye tooth and Why surgeons do the bone graft

q5.answer: At about 8 to 11 years old, but the team chooses the time by how far the teeth have grown, not by age.
q5.where: Sheet 1, When surgeons do the graft

q6.answer: Most often from the hip (soft, spongy bone).

q7.answer: New bone fills the gap and the gum has healed over it. The eye tooth is a little lower and moves down toward the graft.
q7.where: Sheet 2, key message box and What has changed

q8.answer: With an X-ray at about 3 to 6 months after surgery. It shows how well the new bone has taken.

q9.answer: Your hip can be sore for a while. In one study children went back to school about 2 weeks after surgery.

q10.answer: The eye tooth has come down through the new bone (the graft) and is fully in the row of teeth. Some get stuck and need a small operation.

q11.answer: Fixed braces line up the teeth. Almost everyone who has this graft needs them.

q12.answer: Two plans. 1) Close the space: braces move the eye tooth into the place of the missing tooth, and the dentist reshapes it. This is used most often. 2) Keep the space: a plate you can take out holds a false tooth while you grow, then later an implant (post with a crown) or a bridge with one wing glued to the tooth next to the gap. The cleft team talks with you about which plan suits you.
